Do NA-POPS-corrected point counts reproduce spot-mapping densities? Canadian Breeding Bird Census vs BAM

David Iles, assisted by Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol

17 November 2026

1 Summary

What this compares. This repository compares two ways of estimating breeding-bird density in Canada:

  • Point counts from the Boreal Avian Modelling (BAM) Project’s point-count database, converted to density with detectability corrections from NA-POPS (Point count Offsets for Population Sizes of North American landbirds).
  • Spot mapping from the Canadian Breeding Bird Census (CBBC), in which observers visited fixed plots repeatedly and mapped territories, giving densities that need no detectability correction.

If the NA-POPS corrections are about right, corrected point counts near CBBC plots should give densities of the same magnitude as the CBBC censuses. It is a plausibility check on the corrections, not a validation of them; the limitations are set out in Section 2.2.

The same check is repeated with the older Partners in Flight (PIF) corrections that NA-POPS replaced in continental population estimates (a time-of-day adjustment instead of availability, and an expert-assigned detection distance instead of EDR), to see which set of corrections brings point counts closer to the CBBC censuses (Section 2.3).

1.1 Key findings

All results below use only the 26 final CBBC locations after excluding every historical plot in a group of identical recorded coordinates. Species must occur in at least 5 of these locations. All numerical results below are computed for this restricted sample.

  • NA-POPS-corrected point counts vs spot mapping. For the 31 comparable species, NA-POPS-corrected point-count density is a median of 1.48 times the CBBC territory density (plot-averaged density ratio). Individual species are typically 1.73-fold from agreement in either direction; 55% are within 2× and 100% within 10× (Section 2.1).
  • PIF vs NA-POPS. The older PIF corrections assume each survey samples a median of 4.02 times as many birds as NA-POPS does, so they give lower densities. With PIF the median density ratio is 0.34, against 1.48 with NA-POPS, so on the median NA-POPS is closer to agreement. PIF is closer for 13 of 31 comparable species (Section 2.3).
  • Composition. Before any correction, CBBC and BAM relative abundances have a Spearman correlation of 0.62 across species. Uncorrected and NA-POPS-corrected abundance have a Spearman correlation of 0.89 across species, which measures how much the corrections re-rank species (Section 4.7).
pif_density_ratio |>
  filter(species %in% species_order, correction %in% c("NA-POPS", "PIF")) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order)) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = ratio, y = species)) +
  ref_vlines() +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(group = species), colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(colour = correction, shape = correction), size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = RATIO_BREAKS, labels = fold_labels) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = CORRECTION_COLOURS) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = CORRECTION_SHAPES) +
  labs(x = "Plot-averaged density ratio: corrected point-count density / CBBC density", y = NULL, colour = NULL, shape = NULL,
       caption = REF_CAPTION) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

1.2 How to read these results

This is a plausibility check on the NA-POPS corrections, not a validation of them. A ratio near 1 means corrected point counts give densities of the same magnitude as an independent, intensive census. Even with perfect corrections the ratio need not be 1:

  • Birds vs territories. Point counts may include non-territorial individuals, while spot mapping records territories, so ratios somewhat above 1 are expected.
  • Time. The censuses and the point counts are a median of 29 years apart (Section 5.4), and populations have changed in between.
  • Habitat. Points within 1 km of a plot can sample habitat the plot does not represent. Point counts in this analysis therefore represent a broader collection of habitats than CBBC plots that were selected within relatively uniform habitats.

The 95% intervals are sampling intervals: they take the NA-POPS corrections and CBBC densities as given, and do not include uncertainty in the corrections, which is dominated by EDR (Section 6). Section 2.2 sets out what moves the ratios.

How this report is organized. Section 2 gives the main results and Section 3 the methods in brief. The checks on those results (Section 4), the data behind them (Section 5) and the NA-POPS corrections themselves (Section 6) follow. The appendix (Section 7) has a worked example of the calculations, the data sources, how to reproduce the analysis and all the code.

2 Main results

2.1 NA-POPS-corrected point counts vs spot mapping

What this shows. For each species, the mean NA-POPS-corrected point-count density across all its matched CBBC grids, divided by the mean CBBC territory density over the same grids (the plot-averaged density ratio; Section 3.3). Each plot contributes equally, however many surveys it has. Grids where spot mapping found no territories of a species add their corrected density to the numerator only, and the per-species table shows how much of each species’ corrected density comes from them. Intervals come from the site bootstrap. A species with no birds counted gets a ratio of 0 with a degenerate interval here, so use its count-ratio interval instead (Section 4.1).

plot_pair(df = density_ratio, x = "den_mean", y = "num_mean",

Figure 2.2: Species mean densities across all matched grids: NA-POPS-corrected point counts vs CBBC.

For comparable species, the median plot-averaged density ratio is 1.48, with a median fold difference of 1.73 in either direction, 55% of species within 2× of agreement and 100% within 10×.

How to read:

  • Systematic bias vs scatter. The median ratio shows whether corrected point counts run systematically above or below CBBC densities; the median fold difference shows how far individual species typically are from agreement in either direction. A median near 1 with large scatter means no overall bias but poor species-level agreement.
  • Grids without CBBC territories. A large share of a species’ corrected density from these grids means it was often counted near plots where spot mapping found none: either the points sample habitat the plot does not represent (most likely for edge and early-successional species), or the species colonized those plots after the census. Either way, its ratio is raised by something other than detectability.
  • Agreement across plots. The median Spearman correlation across plots shows whether, within a species, corrected densities are higher where CBBC densities are higher. Each site’s point-count density rests on few surveys (Table 5.5), so low correlations are expected even if the corrections are right.

2.2 What the ratios do and do not show

A ratio of 1 means NA-POPS-corrected counts reproduce CBBC territory densities on average for that species. It does not, on its own, show that availability and EDR are right, because other things move the ratios:

  • non-territorial birds contribute to point counts but not to spot-mapped territories
  • spot mapping also misses some territories; point counts in this analysis often sample habitat the CBBC plot does not represent
  • populations have changed in the several decades that elapsed between the CBBC and point count surveys

The detection-rate check (Section 4) complements both ratios, because it compares how often surveys detect the species at all, which pairs and family groups do not inflate.

2.3 PIF corrections instead of NA-POPS

Question. Before NA-POPS, Partners in Flight (PIF) continental population estimates (Blancher et al. 2013; Stanton et al. 2019) converted Breeding Bird Survey counts to densities with two species-level corrections: a time-of-day adjustment, since replaced by NA-POPS availability, and a maximum detection distance (MDD), since replaced by the NA-POPS EDR. Do the PIF corrections bring point counts closer to, or further from, what CBBC densities predict?

How it is calculated. Exactly as for NA-POPS: the same surveys, grids and CBBC densities; only each survey’s effective area changes (Section 3.4). Two hybrid corrections swap one component at a time, to show which replacement matters.

Figure 2.3: Species mean densities across all matched grids: NA-POPS-corrected (left) and PIF-corrected (right) point counts vs CBBC, species with PIF values. CBBC densities are the same in both panels; only the corrected densities change.

37 of the 37 species compared have PIF values. For comparable species, PIF corrections expect a median of 4.02 times as many birds as NA-POPS (Table 2.3), so they give correspondingly lower corrected densities. The median plot-averaged density ratio is 0.34 with PIF corrections and 1.48 with NA-POPS, with median fold differences from agreement of 2.97 and 1.73, and 32% and 55% of species within 2× of agreement, respectively (Table 2.4). PIF brings 13 of 31 comparable species closer to agreement (42%; exact 95% interval 25%-61%). With plots weighted by survey effort instead, the median count ratio is 0.42 with PIF and 1.61 with NA-POPS (Table 4.4).

How to read:

  • Which way PIF moves the ratios. In Table 2.3, values above 1 mean PIF assumes the surveys sample more birds than NA-POPS does, which lowers corrected densities and the density ratio (and, in a population estimate, the population). In Figure 2.3, this moves every species down from its NA-POPS position by about that factor: a factor shared by all species shifts the cloud of points off the 1:1 line without changing its scatter. The two hybrid rows split the difference into its two parts: time of day instead of availability, and MDD instead of EDR. Effective area grows with the square of the detection radius, so MDD vs EDR usually dominates for unlimited-distance counts, where it changes the area by (MDD / EDR)². For counts truncated at 50 or 100 m, both areas approach the truncation circle (π r²) when the radius is well beyond the limit, so the distance part shrinks.
  • Closer to 1 is not automatically better. As Section 2.2 explains, the density ratio would sit below 1 even with perfect corrections if populations had declined since the census, and above 1 where pairs, fledglings and non-territorial birds are counted, or where points near a plot sample habitat the plot does not represent. A correction that moves ratios toward 1 is better only if those effects are small. In particular, if NA-POPS ratios already run above 1, PIF corrections can look better partly by offsetting the counting of individuals against territories, rather than by being better detectability corrections.
  • Hybrids. If a hybrid agrees better than both full sets (Table 2.4), one component of each set is closer to the census than the other: for example, NA-POPS availability with PIF MDD agreeing best would point to EDR, not availability, as the source of any NA-POPS inflation.
  • Uncertainty. As elsewhere, the intervals are sampling intervals that take the corrections as given. The PIF corrections carry no uncertainty here, and the time-of-day value refers to BBS timing rather than each BAM survey’s own date and time.

3 Methods in brief

3.1 Data and matching

Point counts. Human point counts from the BAM database (no ARU recordings, no eBird checklists), within 1 km of retained CBBC plots, in the breeding season and in the morning (filters in P2_match_bam_surveys.R; Table 5.2). All plots in coordinate groups containing multiple distinct CBBC SITEIDs were excluded before assignment, because their identical recorded positions cannot identify which historical plot nearby surveys represent. Among the initially survey-matched plots, this excluded 15 plots in 3 coordinate groups; 26 uniquely located CBBC sites remain. Each retained BAM survey is assigned once to its nearest eligible plot in P2, before species selection.

Why spot mapping. CBBC observers visited each plot repeatedly (at least the minimum number of visits set in P1; Table 5.1) and mapped territories, so CBBC densities are territories per unit area, including fractions of territories crossing the plot edge, with no detectability correction involved. For territorial songbirds detected mainly by song, this is approximately the quantity a corrected point count estimates. The two are not identical: point counts record individuals (which may include non-territorial individuals), whereas spot mapping records territories. Spot mapping also misses some territories, so CBBC is treated as an independent reference rather than the truth.

Sites compared. Every comparison uses the final matched, coordinate-unambiguous CBBC sites for every species, including sites where spot mapping found no territories of that species (CBBC density 0). The species occurrence threshold is also evaluated on exactly these final sites. Two things argue for including sites with CBBC zeros:

  • No selection on the outcome. Keeping only grids where spot mapping found a species selects grids where its CBBC density was high partly by chance, and biases CBBC densities upward relative to the point counts.
  • Turnover since the census. Over the decades between the censuses and the point counts, species were lost from some plots and gained at others. Keeping only grids where the species held territories at the census keeps the losses but discards the gains, which biases point-count densities downward. Including all retained sites allows both apparent losses and gains to contribute, although spatially heterogeneous change, imperfect census coverage and habitat differences remain.

The cost is habitat mismatch: points within 1 km of a plot can sample habitat the plot does not represent (for example, edges or young forest around a mature-forest plot), so a species can be counted near a plot where spot mapping found none.

3.2 Species compared

Scope. Species are selected if CBBC territories were recorded at 5 or more of the 26 final, uniquely located sites (set in P3), and an NA-POPS model is available, without which counts cannot be corrected. Nothing about BAM detections, availability or EDR is used, so no species is included or excluded because of how well BAM and CBBC agree. Results are summarised for all species and for comparable species separately. A species was considered non-comparable if spot-mapped territories are likely to be a poor proxy for one bird on a point count: e.g., non-territorial, flocking, or species whose territories are far larger than the plots). The list is tentative and subjective, and set in script P1 (non_comparable_species in Section 7.5.

37 of 39 candidate species have NA-POPS models and are compared (31 comparable, 6 non-comparable). 0 of them were never detected by a matched BAM survey. The species are listed in Table 5.8.

3.3 How point counts are compared with CBBC

Effective area. NA-POPS converts a point count to a density by dividing it by the area the survey effectively sampled. For survey j:

Aj = pj × π × EDR² × (1 − exp(−(rj / EDR)²)) / 106 (km²)

where pj is availability, the probability that a bird present sings or calls during the count (NA-POPS removal model; it depends on the survey’s duration, day of year and time since sunrise), EDR is the species’ effective detection radius (m; NA-POPS intercept-only distance model), and rj is the survey’s distance limit (m). For an unlimited-distance count the last factor is 1.

Plot-averaged density ratio (main comparison). For each species and CBBC grid g, the corrected point-count density is Bg = Σ count / Σ Aj over the surveys assigned to the grid. The CBBC density Dg is territories on the plot divided by plot area, averaged over the grid’s census years. The species’ ratio is R = mean(Bg) / mean(Dg) over all its matched grids, so R = 1 means corrected point counts reproduce CBBC territory densities on average. Every plot gets equal weight, whatever its number of surveys. That matters here because survey effort ranges from one survey to well over 100 per site (Table 5.5).

Count ratio (check). Birds counted divided by birds expected, Σ count / Σ (Aj × Dg), over the species’ surveys. It is the maximum-likelihood estimate under a Poisson model, but weights each plot by its survey effort, so one heavily surveyed plot can dominate it.

Intervals. The 95% sampling intervals come from a site bootstrap: sites are resampled with all their surveys, so repeat visits and nearby points move together. They describe how much the results depend on which sites and surveys happened to be available, taking the NA-POPS corrections and the CBBC densities as given. They do not include uncertainty in the corrections themselves (model choice, NA-POPS release, availability), error in the historical CBBC densities, population change or spatial mismatch. Because density scales with 1 / EDR² for unlimited-distance counts, errors in EDR dominate that uncertainty (Section 6).

The appendix (Section 7.1) works through both ratios with a small invented example, and explains how plot size and survey effort enter them.

3.4 PIF corrections

PIF converts counts to densities with a time-of-day adjustment instead of availability, and a maximum detection distance (MDD) instead of EDR. The PIF effective area (computed in P4_pif_corrections.R) is:

AjPIF = pjPIF × π × MDD² × (1 − exp(−(rj / MDD)²)) / 106

  • MDD (m) is the PIF detection distance, treated here as an expert-elicited estimate of the species’ EDR, so the formula is the NA-POPS one with MDD in place of EDR. Despite the name “maximum detection distance”, PIF uses it as the radius of the area a count samples (π × MDD²), the role EDR plays in NA-POPS. The PIF handbook (version 3.1) acknowledges that not all birds within that distance are detected, notes that its distance classes tend to run larger than empirical effective detection distances, and names replacing them with EDRs as the next step. With the same half-normal detection function for both, PIF and NA-POPS differ only in the value of the radius. For unlimited-distance counts the area is pjPIF × π × MDD².
  • pjPIF comes from the PIF time-of-day value T: the share of birds counted at the mean BBS time of day relative to the species’ peak time, on a 3-min BBS stop. BAM surveys last 3 to 10 min, so T is rescaled to each survey’s duration d (min) assuming a constant cue rate, pPIF = 1 − (1 − T)d/3, the same rescaling used for the 5-min availability in Table 5.8 (setting pif_scale_duration in P4: TRUE; if FALSE, T is used unchanged for every survey). Unlike NA-POPS availability, it does not change with date or time since sunrise.
  • The PIF pair adjustment is not used. PIF multiplies densities by a pair adjustment (1 to 2) to convert birds counted to individuals. NA-POPS did not replace it, and both comparisons here set birds counted against territories, so leaving it out means any difference between the NA-POPS and PIF ratios comes only from the two corrections that NA-POPS replaced. Species with a pair adjustment below 2 are, by PIF’s own reckoning, counted as more than one bird per territory (both sexes, or family groups), so their ratios should run above 1 under either set of corrections.
  • Hybrids. To show which replacement matters, two hybrid corrections swap one component at a time: PIF time of day with the NA-POPS EDR, and NA-POPS availability with the PIF MDD.

Corrections that assume a survey samples more birds give lower corrected densities, a lower density ratio, and smaller populations. For one species, the PIF count ratio divided by the NA-POPS count ratio equals birds expected with NA-POPS divided by birds expected with PIF. The plot-averaged density ratio moves by about the same factor, though not exactly, because the PIF / NA-POPS effective-area ratio varies somewhat between surveys of one species (with duration and distance limit).

4 Supporting analyses and robustness checks

These analyses check whether the main results depend on how plots are weighted, on how many birds are recorded per detection, on the time since the census and on plot characteristics, and compare species composition.

4.1 Count ratio: plots weighted by survey effort

What this shows. For each species, the total number of birds counted by its surveys divided by the total expected from CBBC density and each survey’s NA-POPS effective area (the observed and expected counts of Table 5.8). It weights each grid by its survey effort multiplied by its CBBC density, so it checks whether the plot-averaged result holds when every survey counts equally, and shows where a few heavily surveyed grids dominate.

4.4 Detection-rate check

What this tests. A second check that is insensitive to how many birds were recorded per detection. If CBBC density and the NA-POPS corrections were both right, a survey with effective area a would detect the species (count at least one bird) with probability 1 − exp(−DCBBC × a). The observed share of surveys detecting the species is compared with this expectation. It is evaluated per survey, not per grid, because repeat visits to the same point re-survey the same birds. At grids where spot mapping found no territories the expected detection rate is 0, so any detection there counts as excess.

kable(detection_summary, digits = 2,
      caption = "Detection-rate check at all matched grids (comparable species): observed vs expected share of surveys detecting the species", label = "step3-detection-1")

  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_point(colour = CLASS_COLOURS[["Comparable"]], shape = CLASS_SHAPES[["Comparable"]]) +
  geom_text(mapping = aes(label = species), size = 2.2, vjust = -0.7, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Expected share of surveys detecting the species (CBBC density x NA-POPS area)",
       y = "Observed share of surveys detecting the species",
       caption = "Line: agreement") +
  theme_bw()

Figure 4.2: Detection-rate check, comparable species at all matched grids: observed vs expected share of surveys detecting the species.

Across all matched grids, surveys detected species a median 9% of the time, against 5% expected.

How to read: if the detection rate matches expectation while the density ratio is above 1, the excess comes from more birds per detection (pairs, family groups), not from the detection probabilities. Detections at grids without CBBC territories raise the observed rate, for the same reasons they raise the density ratio (habitat around the plots, colonization since the census). If surveys detect species less often than expected, they are sampling other habitat, the species has declined, or birds are more clumped than a Poisson count assumes (which lowers the chance of detecting at least one bird for the same mean count).

4.5 Population change since the census

What this tests. Whether the disagreement for each species follows the time between the census and the point counts. This matters most for the question of whether QPAD inflates density. If a species declined by 30% after its census, a correct QPAD estimate would sit at about 0.7× the CBBC density, and a ratio of 1 would itself indicate inflation. Population change therefore masks QPAD inflation for declining species and exaggerates it for increasing ones.

ggplot(data = time_data, mapping = aes(x = median_year_gap, y = ratio)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.5, 2), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  geom_point(colour = CLASS_COLOURS[["Comparable"]], shape = CLASS_SHAPES[["Comparable"]]) +
  geom_text(mapping = aes(label = species), size = 2.2, vjust = -0.7, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = RATIO_BREAKS, labels = fold_labels) +
  labs(x = "Median years between CBBC census and point counts", y = "Plot-averaged density ratio (corrected / CBBC)",
       caption = "Lines: agreement (solid) and 2x (dashed)") +
  theme_bw()

Figure 4.3: Plot-averaged density ratio vs median years between the CBBC census and the point counts, by species.

How to read: a trend in the density ratio with years since the census points to population change (or changing census methods) rather than detectability. The time gap alone cannot separate the two: correcting for it would need each species’ population trend over the census-to-survey period.

4.6 Which plots disagree most?

What this tests: which site characteristics are associated with larger disagreement:

  • plot size (a control; see below for why it cannot be read as an edge effect);
  • census effort (visits per census);
  • census year (older census methods, or population change).

Each site’s community ratio sums all comparable species at the site, whether or not spot mapping found them there: summed NA-POPS-corrected BAM density divided by summed CBBC density.

Sites used Number of sites log(plot size) estimate Std. Error Pr(>|t|)
All sites 25 2.904 0.863 0.003
Plots <= 16 ha 22 0.354 1.151 0.762

How to read: these terms capture remaining CBBC census-quality effects (coverage, older methods) and population change since the census.

  • Plot size is a control, not a measured edge effect. Most matched plots are 10–16 ha (Table 5.6): squares with sides of about 316 to 400 m. Over that range the share of a plot lying within one territory radius of its edge changes only modestly (about 53% to 44% for territories 100 m across), so a genuine edge effect could not change the ratio by more than a little. A large plot-size coefficient is therefore more likely to reflect a few larger plots with high leverage, or plots of different sizes differing in habitat, region or era. Table 4.7 shows how much the coefficient depends on the plots larger than 16 ha. Any tendency to over-count edge territories affects almost every matched plot similarly, so it cannot be estimated from these plot sizes.
  • Plot habitat is not included. Habitat mismatch between a plot and its nearby points shows up as BAM detections of species absent from the plot, which raise the site’s community ratio. The regression does not separate this from the other causes of disagreement.
  • Matching radius. The 1 km matching radius was chosen over 2 km because density declined about 11% from 0-1 km to 1-2 km at the same sites, as habitat shifted away from the plot’s.

4.7 Composition: do the datasets agree on which species are common?

What this tests: whether, before any correction, the two methods rank species similarly. This is the most robust comparison in the report: it needs no detectability correction and no units, so errors in NA-POPS cannot affect it. Strong agreement means the datasets describe broadly the same communities, so later absolute differences are more likely to reflect detectability. Weak agreement means time, habitat and method differences are large, and the absolute comparisons need more caution.

Relative abundance is computed site by site, then averaged across sites:

  1. Within each matched site, each species’ share of the site’s community: its CBBC territory density divided by the summed density of all species compared at that site, and likewise its BAM uncorrected count per survey divided by the site’s summed count per survey. A species absent from a site has a share of 0 there.
  2. Across sites, each species’ shares are averaged. Only sites where both datasets recorded at least one of the species compared are used, so both averages come from the same sites.

A species whose presence at a site is unknown (missing from an incomplete census list; Table 5.4) is left out of that site’s shares in both datasets, so unknowns are not counted as absences. Each site contributes equally, whatever its plot size or density, and a few plots with exceptionally high densities of one species (for example Bay-breasted Warbler on budworm-outbreak plots) cannot dominate the result. Averaging summed densities instead would let those plots set the species’ share. No detectability correction or units are involved.

kable(cor_1e, digits = 2, caption = "Correlation across species of CBBC and uncorrected BAM relative abundance (mean within-site shares, all matched sites)", label = "step1e-1")

All species 37 0.64 0.62
Comparable 31 0.69 0.69

Shares are averaged over 25 matched sites. Across species, CBBC and uncorrected BAM relative abundances have Spearman ρ = 0.62 (Pearson on log scale 0.64). Within individual sites, the median rank correlation across species is 0.41 (25 sites). How to read: a strong species-level correlation means the datasets broadly agree on community composition before any correction. Species far off the 1:1 line in Figure 4.4 are the candidates for detectability or methodological differences: loud, far-detected species should sit above it (over-represented in counts), and quiet or short-range species below.

4.8 Composition: does correction improve agreement with CBBC?

What this tests: whether applying the NA-POPS corrections makes the BAM species composition more like CBBC’s. This tests the corrections’ relative values between species (for example, that a quiet species needs a larger correction than a loud one), independent of their absolute level. If the corrections were noise, agreement would not improve.

Figure 4.5: CBBC density vs uncorrected (left) and NA-POPS-corrected (right) BAM point counts, species means across all matched grids.

How to read: if the corrected correlation with CBBC is higher, NA-POPS moves species’ relative abundances toward the census. That is independent support for the corrections, separate from their absolute level. In this dataset the correction has little room to do so:

  • How much species differ. Among comparable species, mean counts per survey differ about 280-fold from the least to the most counted species, and CBBC densities about 27-fold. Their corrections (median effective area) differ only about 7.1-fold. On the log scale, counts vary across species with a standard deviation of 1.14, and corrections with 0.44, about 39% as much.
  • Judge the change by its interval. The 95% intervals for the change in correlation (Table 4.10) run from -0.13 to 0.28 for Spearman and from -0.08 to 0.19 for Pearson on the log scale. With 31 species, a correlation of about 0.5 has a standard error of roughly 0.15, so a change of a few hundredths in either direction is noise.
  • What this means. Here, the differences between species in how their counts compare with CBBC are driven far more by ecology than by detectability, so this composition test has little power to judge the corrections. The absolute comparisons (Section 2) are more informative about them.

4.9 Composition with PIF corrections

Systematic shift vs species-level agreement. PIF and NA-POPS can differ in level (median density ratio) and in how they treat species relative to each other. Tables 4.11 and 4.12 test the second: whether PIF’s species-specific values rank species’ densities more like CBBC. PIF MDD comes in a few classes (50 to 400 m), so species in the same class get the same distance correction, and the classes span a wider range than NA-POPS EDRs.

5 Data support

How much matched data there is, how well replicated, from when and where. Every comparison in this report inherits these sample sizes, the time gap and the geographic coverage.

5.1 Sample sizes

What this tests: how many CBBC census records survive the original quality filters, and how many retained sites remain eligible after the separate shared-coordinate exclusion and BAM survey filters. P1 retains the full census-quality audit; P2 records the coordinate exclusion as an additional survey-matching stage. These exclusions are based on distinct CBBC SITEIDs having identical site coordinates, not on all coordinates rounded to minutes or on whether a bird was detected.

149 of 928 census records (112 sites) pass the initial CBBC quality filters. The BAM matching then excludes every CBBC plot whose retained site coordinates are shared with another distinct SITEID. Among plots with eligible nearby surveys, 15 sites at 3 identical-coordinate groups are excluded. This removes 55 distinct BAM surveys that have no match to a remaining eligible site. The resulting 26 final CBBC sites each have at least one assigned BAM survey within 1 km; no survey is counted twice. All downstream species selection and comparisons use precisely this final site set, with a minimum species occurrence threshold of 5 sites. Spatial matching remains approximate even among uniquely recorded coordinate locations.

5.4 Timing

What this tests: how far apart in time the two datasets are. Populations change, so a long gap means CBBC densities may not describe the community the BAM surveys sampled. 6 NA-POPS detectability corrections

Question: how large are the NA-POPS corrections for these species and surveys, and what drives them?

What this tests: this step does not compare with CBBC. It sets expectations for the comparisons with CBBC: a correction can only change agreement with CBBC as much as it varies between species, and the absolute comparisons are only as reliable as the least certain part of the correction.

Each survey’s effective area is p × π × EDR² × (1 − exp(−(r/EDR)²)). Availability p comes from the best NA-POPS removal model (duration, day of year, time since sunrise). EDR comes from the NA-POPS intercept-only distance model: one EDR per species, averaged over the habitats and road types in the NA-POPS training data. Habitat-specific EDRs, using forest cover around each survey, changed densities by a median of about 3%, so they are not used. Each species’ availability and EDR are shown in Table 5.8.

NA-POPS results release: 2024-03-05.

kable(corrections_features, col.names = c("Key feature of the corrections", "Value"),
      caption = "Key features of the NA-POPS corrections for the species compared", label = "step2-stats-1")
Table 6.1: Key features of the NA-POPS corrections for the species compared
Key feature of the corrections Value
Spread of median effective area across species (max / min) 7.1
Share of variance in log effective area due to species identity 74%
Share of between-species variance in log(p x EDR^2) from EDR 81%
Spearman rank correlation, uncorrected vs corrected species abundance 0.89
Median width of density 95% interval from EDR sampling error alone (factor; excludes model, release and availability uncertainty) 1.02
Median share of surveys outside NA-POPS training range 0%

How to read:

  • Spread across species. The corrections differ about 7-fold between species, so they can substantially re-order species. A rank correlation of 0.89 between uncorrected and corrected abundance shows how much they actually do.
  • Within vs between species. Every survey × species combination has its own effective area, and these vary in two ways:
    • Between species. Each species has its own EDR and its own availability model (how often it sings or calls).
    • Within a species, between surveys. Availability depends on each survey’s duration, day of year and time since sunrise, and a distance limit truncates the area sampled (a 50 m count samples much less than an unlimited-distance one). For a typical species, the survey at the 90th percentile of effective area samples about 1.9 times the area of the survey at the 10th percentile.
    “Species identity explains 74%” is the R² of a regression of log effective area on species alone. It means that 74% of all the variation in log effective area, across every survey and species, is accounted for by differences between species’ average effective areas. The remaining 26% is variation among surveys of the same species, from survey protocol (duration, distance limit) and timing (date, time of day). With one EDR per species, none of the within-species variation comes from EDR. So the corrections act mostly between species, setting composition and absolute level. Within a species they mainly put surveys run under different protocols on a common footing, and barely change how sites rank.
  • EDR dominates. EDR enters squared, and accounts for 81% of the between-species variation, so errors in EDR matter most.
  • Precision. EDR sampling error alone gives each species’ density a 95% interval spanning a factor of only about 1.02. That greatly understates the real uncertainty, which also includes the choice of distance model, availability, and the NA-POPS release (which has shifted closed-forest EDRs by up to ~25% between releases). For an unlimited-distance count, density scales with 1 / EDR², so a 25% larger EDR lowers density by 1 − 1/1.25² ≈ 36%, and every comparison with CBBC would shift by about that factor.

7 Appendix

7.1 How the absolute comparisons work

The absolute comparisons use no statistical model. They compare the birds the BAM surveys actually counted with the birds they should have counted if CBBC densities and the NA-POPS corrections were both right. This section explains the logic, with a small invented example, before the results.

7.1.1 The question

NA-POPS turns a point count into a density by dividing the count by the area the survey effectively sampled. Turn that around: if we knew the true density at a place, we could predict how many birds a point count there should record. The comparisons ask how close the counts come to that prediction. For a survey j assigned to CBBC grid g, the working assumption is

E[countj] = k × Aj × Dg

where Dg is the CBBC territory density at the grid (territories / km²), Aj is the survey’s NA-POPS effective area (km²), and k is a single number per species. If the CBBC densities still describe the area the points sample, and the NA-POPS corrections are right, then k = 1. If k = 2, the point counts recorded twice as many birds as CBBC density and NA-POPS together predict.

7.1.2 The ingredients

CBBC density, Dg. Territories on the plot divided by plot area (× 100 to convert from ha to km²). A plot with 3 territories on 10 ha has D = 30 territories / km². If a grid was censused in several years, Dg is the mean across those years. All matched grids are used for every species, including grids where spot mapping found no territories of it (Dg = 0; Section 3.1).

Effective area, Aj. The area within which the survey would have detected every bird if detection were perfect. It combines availability (the chance a bird sings or calls during the count, which depends on the count’s duration, date and time of day), the species’ effective detection radius (EDR), and the survey’s distance limit; the formula is in Section 3.3. For a species with EDR = 80 m, a 5-min unlimited-distance count with availability 0.8 has A = 0.8 × π × 0.08² ≈ 0.016 km² (about 1.6 ha). The same count truncated at 50 m has A ≈ 0.005 km², because only 1 − exp(−(50/80)²) ≈ 32% of the effective area lies within 50 m. That truncated count is expected to record about a third as many birds, which is exactly what truncation does to the observed count, so surveys run under different protocols are put on the same footing.

Which surveys go with which grid. Every retained BAM survey within 1 km of a CBBC plot is assigned to the nearest plot, so a survey within 1 km of two plots is counted once, never twice.

7.1.3 From counts to the two ratios

The two absolute comparisons combine the same surveys and the same CBBC densities in two ways, which differ only in how much weight each plot gets (see “Two ways to weight plots” below). The plot-averaged density ratio is the main comparison; the count ratio is the check.

Plot-averaged density ratio. For each species:

  1. Corrected density at each grid: Bg = Σ count / Σ Aj over the grid’s surveys (birds / km²).
  2. Ratio of means: R = mean(Bg) / mean(Dg), with both means over the same grids.

Grids where spot mapping found no territories add their corrected density to the numerator and nothing to the denominator.

Count ratio. For each species:

  1. Expected count of each survey: Ej = Aj × Dg.
  2. Totals: sum the expected counts over all the species’ surveys, and sum the observed counts over the same surveys.
  3. Count ratio: k = Σ observed / Σ expected.

The ratio of totals is not an arbitrary choice. If counts are Poisson with mean k × Ej, the log-likelihood is Σ [Oj log(k Ej) − k Ej], and setting its derivative to zero gives k = ΣOj / ΣEj: the ratio of totals is the maximum-likelihood estimate. Overdispersion (pairs or family groups counted together, clumped birds) does not bias it; it only makes it less precise, which the confidence intervals below take into account. Averaging each survey’s own ratio instead would fail badly: most surveys record none of a given species against expected counts of a fraction of a bird, so their individual ratios would be 0, or very large when a single bird turned up.

7.1.4 A worked example

An invented species, with A ≈ 0.016 km² for every survey (in the real data A varies a little between surveys). Spot mapping found no territories at G4:

Grid Plot size Territories on plot D (/ km²) Surveys Expected Observed Corrected density B (/ km²)
G1 10 ha 3 30 2 2 × 0.016 × 30 = 0.96 1 1 / (2 × 0.016) = 31.3
G2 100 ha 15 15 40 40 × 0.016 × 15 = 9.60 20 31.3
G3 40 ha 4 10 8 8 × 0.016 × 10 = 1.28 1 7.8
G4 20 ha 0 0 6 0 1 10.4
Total / mean mean 13.75 56 11.84 23 mean 20.2
  • Plot-averaged density ratio: R = 20.2 / 13.75 ≈ 1.47.
  • Count ratio: k = 23 / 11.84 ≈ 1.94.

Without G4, the two ratios would be 1.28 and 1.86. G4’s one bird adds to both numerators but to neither denominator, because the CBBC census found no territories there.

The count ratio (1.94) is close to G2’s own ratio (20 / 9.60 = 2.08), even though G1 and G3 both suggest agreement. The reason is visible if k is rewritten as a weighted average of the grid ratios of the grids with territories, k = Σg wg kg (plus G4’s birds on top), where each grid’s weight wg is its share of the total expected count: 8% for G1, 81% for G2 and 11% for G3. A grid’s expected count is (number of surveys) × (effective area) × (CBBC density), so a grid’s influence on the count ratio is proportional to its survey effort multiplied by its CBBC density. The plot-averaged density ratio drops survey effort from the weights.

7.1.5 CBBC plots of very different sizes

Plot size does not weight either ratio directly. It enters only through density, which already divides territories by plot area. In the example, G1 (10 ha) and G2 (100 ha) are weighted by their surveys and densities, not their sizes: had G1 been a 100 ha plot with 30 territories, its density, and everything downstream, would be unchanged. That is usually what we want, because the BAM surveys sample the 1 km circle around a plot (about 314 ha) regardless of how large the plot is.

Plot size still matters in three ways that neither ratio adjusts for, because both treat CBBC density as known:

  • Precision of the density. On a 10 ha plot, one territory more or less changes density by 10 / km², so G1’s 30 / km² could easily have been 20 or 40. On a 100 ha plot, one territory changes density by 1 / km².
  • Edge effects. Territories straddling the plot boundary are counted as fractions, and a “+” (part of a territory) is coded as 0.1 territory, which on a 10 ha plot is 1 territory / km² on its own. Small plots tend to overstate density because edge territories make up a larger share of them.
  • Habitat match. A 10 ha plot is about 3% of the 1 km matching circle, so the points around it can easily sample habitat the plot does not represent; a 100 ha plot covers about a third of the circle (Table 5.6).

So small plots bring noisier, possibly inflated and less representative densities into both ratios, but no extra weight. This is why P1 drops plots under 10 ha, and why plot size is a term in the site-level regression (Section 4.6).

7.1.6 CBBC plots with very different numbers of point counts

Survey effort does weight the count ratio directly: doubling the surveys at a grid doubles both its observed and expected totals, and so doubles its weight. That is reasonable when the extra surveys carry extra information (more points spread around the plot, or more years), and less so when they mostly repeat the same few points. In these data the busiest CBBC site has well over 100 retained surveys while the median site has a handful (Table 5.5), so one site can decide a species’ count ratio almost on its own, as G2 does in the example. This is the main reason the plot-averaged density ratio, which gives a plot with 2 surveys the same weight as one with 100, is the main comparison in this report. The count-ratio table (Table 4.2) reports the share of each species’ expected count that comes from its single largest site, to show where the count ratio is dominated by one site.

Repeat visits to the same point are not independent either: the same territorial birds are counted visit after visit, so 40 surveys at G2 may amount to a few independent samples of the birds around one location. This does not bias either ratio, but a naive Poisson standard error would be far too small. The 95% sampling intervals of both ratios therefore come from a site bootstrap:

  1. Draw sites at random, with replacement, as many as the species has.
  2. Keep all of each drawn site’s surveys together, so repeat visits and nearby points move as a block.
  3. Recompute the ratio for that resample.
  4. Repeat 1000 times; the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resampled ratios form the 95% interval.

Because whole sites are resampled, the interval reflects how much the result depends on which sites happened to be surveyed, including clustering and overdispersion. It also exposes dominance by one site. In the example, about a third of resamples contain no copy of G2 ((3/4)⁴ ≈ 32%), and in those the count ratio comes from G1, G3 and G4 alone, about 3 / 2.24 ≈ 1.3; resamples containing G2, sometimes twice, give about 2. The count ratio’s bootstrap distribution has two peaks and its interval becomes wide and lopsided, sometimes with the point estimate near one end. A resample that draws only grids without CBBC territories (here, G4 four times) has an undefined ratio and is dropped; this matters only for species found by spot mapping at very few grids. With fewer than about 10 grids with territories, or one dominant site, treat an interval as a rough guide rather than a reliable 95% interval.

The bootstrap breaks down when few or no birds were counted. For the plot-averaged density ratio this gives a ratio of 0 with a degenerate interval; use the count-ratio interval for such species. For the count ratio, if no site recorded the species, every resample gives a count ratio of 0, and the interval collapses to 0–0 even though, say, 20 birds were expected; a zero count is still consistent with a true ratio above 0. So the reported count-ratio interval is the wider of the bootstrap interval and the exact Poisson interval for the total count, divided by the expected count. With no birds counted, the exact Poisson upper bound on the total is about 3.7 birds, so with 20 expected the upper bound of the count ratio is about 0.18. The Poisson interval ignores clustering, which is why it is used only to widen the bootstrap interval, never to narrow it.

7.1.7 Two ways to weight plots

The plot-averaged density ratio first converts each grid’s counts to a corrected density (Σ count / Σ effective area at that grid), then divides the mean of those densities across grids by the mean CBBC density across the same grids. Over the grids with territories, this works out to a weighted average of the grid ratios with weights proportional to CBBC density alone, ignoring survey effort. Grids without territories add their corrected density on top, in both ratios:

Comparison Weights (G1 / G2 / G3) Result in the example
Plot-averaged density ratio (main) 55% / 27% / 18% (CBBC density only) (31.3 + 31.3 + 7.8 + 10.4) / (30 + 15 + 10 + 0) ≈ 1.47
Count ratio (check) 8% / 81% / 11% (survey effort × CBBC density) 23 / 11.84 ≈ 1.94

The two answer slightly different questions. The plot-averaged density ratio asks whether, taking the CBBC plots one at a time, corrected densities matched; a plot with 2 surveys counts as much as one with 100, so it is noisier, but no single site can dominate it through effort alone. The count ratio asks whether, across all the counting that was done, the counts matched the prediction; it uses the survey effort efficiently, and is the maximum-likelihood estimate under a Poisson model, but one heavily surveyed site can dominate it. Survey effort here ranges from one survey to well over 100 per site (Table 5.5), so the plot-averaged density ratio is the main comparison. When the two differ by more than about 2× for a species, one or two heavily surveyed sites are driving the count ratio.

What the ratios do and do not show is discussed in Section 2.2.

7.2 Data sources

None of the data are included in this repository. The scripts read them from local paths set at the top of each script (Section 7.4).

Source What is used Notes
Canadian Breeding Bird Census (CBBC) PLOTS and SPECIES tables: plot location, size, habitat, census year and visits; territory counts per species Database documented in Kennedy et al. (1999), CWS Technical Report 342. Held by Environment and Climate Change Canada (Canadian Wildlife Service). Census records are filtered for coordinate quality, list completeness, effort, plot size, year and habitat in P1_prepare_cbbc.R; sites sharing identical retained coordinates are excluded from BAM matching in P2_match_bam_surveys.R.
BAM point-count database (v5) Human point counts (no ARU recordings, no eBird checklists) within 1 km of each retained CBBC plot, with survey date, time, duration, distance limit and counts DuckDB build 03_BAMDataset_WT-2026-08-26_EBd-Jun-2026_PRISM-2026-10-09. Access through the BAM Project’s data-sharing process.
NA-POPS Species availability (removal) and distance (EDR) models Through the napops R package; the results release used is reported in Section 6. The intercept-only distance model is used.
PIF corrections Population_estimates_workflow_support.xlsx: PIF time-of-day adjustment (PIF_time_of_day), maximum detection distance (PIF_MDD) and pair adjustment (PIF_pair) per species Corrections used in PIF continental population estimates (Blancher et al. 2013; Stanton et al. 2019). Matched to NA-POPS species by common name in P4_pif_corrections.R, where MDD is used as an expert estimate of EDR. The pair adjustment is listed but not used (Section 2.3).
Bird Conservation Regions Boundaries for the site map Optional; the map is drawn without them if the file is absent.

7.3 Repository structure and workflow

spot-mapping-vs-point counts/
├── *.Rproj            RStudio project (sets the project root used by here::here())
├── README.Rmd         this report; knits to README.md and README_files/
├── script/            preparation scripts P1-P4
├── data/              local input data (not included in the repository)
└── output/            cached outputs of P1-P4 (not included in the repository)

The analysis has four preparation scripts, each run once with its output cached, followed by this report:

Step Script Prepares Cached output (in output/)
1 script/P1_prepare_cbbc.R CBBC coordinates, census filters, densities, species-code rules and flags for SITEIDs sharing recorded coordinates P1_cbbc_prepared.rds
2 script/P2_match_bam_surveys.R BAM surveys within 1 km, survey filters, exclusion of entire shared-coordinate groups, unique nearest-site assignment, exclusion audit, and counts P2_bam_matched.rds
3 script/P3_napops_corrections.R Species with CBBC territories at 5 or more final sites, NA-POPS availability, EDR and effective area for every survey and species P3_napops_corrections.rds
4 script/P4_pif_corrections.R PIF time-of-day and maximum-detection-distance effective areas (and two hybrids) for the same surveys and species P4_pif_corrections.rds
5 README.Rmd This report, knitted to README.md figures in README_files/

Each script and the report define their settings as constants at the top, and record them with their outputs; Section 7.5 lists the settings used for this version.

7.4 Reproducing the analysis

  1. Open the RStudio project (the .Rproj file in the repository root). All paths inside the project are built with here::here(), so they resolve from the project root, whichever folder a script is run from.
  2. Place the input data in data/, or set the data paths at the top of each preparation script (CBBC tables in P1, the BAM DuckDB file in P2, the PIF table in P4), and optionally the BCR file at the top of README.Rmd.
  3. Install the R packages used: tidyverse, readxl, sf, DBI, duckdb, suncalc, lutz, napops, rappdirs, here, knitr and bookdown.
  4. Run script/P1_prepare_cbbc.R, script/P2_match_bam_surveys.R, script/P3_napops_corrections.R and script/P4_pif_corrections.R, in that order. Each writes its output to output/. The new P2 excludes shared-coordinate groups and performs nearest-site assignment before P3 selects species at 5 or more final sites. Re-run all four scripts after updating this workflow; older cached .rds files are incompatible. Each later script reads the earlier outputs.
  5. Knit README.Rmd (in the repository root) with the Knit button. This writes both README.html and README.md (and Markdown figures in README_files/); commit the .md and figure folder so GitHub can display the regenerated results. All numerical summaries, tables, confidence intervals and figures are recomputed from the revised caches.

Because the data are not public, README.md shows the results of the author’s local run.
